Fast exact cross-validation for global kriging

Source: R/kcv.R
kcv.Rd

A drop-in companion to gstat::krige.cv() for global kriging (every observation in the kriging neighborhood). Instead of refitting the kriging system once per fold, kcv() factorizes the covariance matrix once and obtains every fold's predictions and variances from it. Results match krige.cv() to numerical precision.

Usage

kcv(
  formula,
  locations,
  data,
  model,
  nfold,
  folds = NULL,
  beta = NULL,
  buffer = NULL,
  targets = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

formula

Formula defining the response and the trend, e.g. log(zinc) ~ 1 or log(zinc) ~ sqrt(dist). A matrix response, such as cbind(log(zinc), log(copper)) ~ 1 or a matrix column of data, cross-validates each column with the same model, trend and folds; see "Several responses" below.

locations

A formula giving the coordinates (e.g. ~x + y) when data is a data.frame, or an sf object or sp Spatial*DataFrame holding both the locations and the variables (then data is not used).

data

A data.frame, when locations is a formula.

model

A gstat variogram model (gstat::vgm()) with fixed parameters. Supported: Nug, Exp, Sph, Gau, Mat, Ste, Cir, Pen, Bes, Wav, Hol and nested sums of them, with optional 2D geometric anisotropy.

nfold

As in gstat::krige.cv(): missing or nrow(data) for leave-one-out; a single integer k < n for random k-fold assignment (drawn exactly as krige.cv() does, so the same seed gives the same folds); or a vector of length n of fold identifiers.

folds

Optional vector of length n of fold identifiers. Takes precedence over nfold.

beta

Optional trend coefficients; if given, simple kriging with this known trend is used. A vector of length p (the number of trend coefficients) is shared by all responses; with several responses, a p x T matrix gives one column of coefficients per response.

buffer

Optional radius for buffered leave-one-out, in coordinate units (\(\ge 0\)). Each observation is predicted from the observations farther than buffer from it; see "Buffered leave-one-out" below. Cannot be combined with nfold or folds.

targets

Optional, with buffer: the observations to predict, as row numbers or a logical vector of length n. The hold-out sets are still formed from all observations. Useful to estimate buffered leave-one-out statistics from a sample of points when the radius is large. By default every observation is predicted.

...

Accepted for compatibility with krige.cv(): verbose and debug.level are ignored. Local-neighborhood or block arguments (nmax, nmin, maxdist, block) are not supported and raise an error.

Value

An object of the same kind as the input (a data.frame with the coordinate columns appended, an sf object, or an sp SpatialPointsDataFrame) with columns var1.pred, var1.var, observed, residual (observed minus predicted), zscore (residual divided by the kriging standard error) and fold, as in krige.cv(). With buffer, fold is the row number (each observation is its own hold-out set) and a column n_heldout gives the number of observations held out for it, itself included; with targets, only the target rows are returned, in increasing row order. With a matrix response, the results of the responses are stacked (all rows of the first response, then the second, ...) and a factor column response, after fold (and n_heldout), names the response of each row.

Details

Ordinary kriging (formula = z ~ 1) and universal kriging (z ~ x + y, external drift, ...) re-estimate the trend by generalized least squares in each fold, as gstat does. Simple kriging is used when beta is supplied.

Several responses

The kriging weights depend only on the locations, the variogram model, the trend and the folds, not on the observed values. A matrix response with T columns is therefore cross-validated from one factorization: each additional response costs a few matrix products (no further factorization), and in buffered leave-one-out the hold-out sets and their factorizations are shared too. Typical uses are many simulated fields, several variables or time slices observed at the same locations, or bootstrap replicates. kcv_run() with y cross-validates new responses from an existing prepared object.

A response with one column (such as scale(z) ~ 1, or a one-column matrix column) is a single response, as in stats::model.response(), unless the left-hand side is an explicit cbind().

Every response is predicted at every location, so a missing or non-finite value in any column is an error. Response names come from the column names, else from the arguments of cbind(), else they are "1", "2", .... Each response's rows are the output of the single-response call, up to rounding in the last bits (with several columns the BLAS uses matrix-matrix products). kcv_metrics() summarizes each response separately. The output holds about \(10 n\) numbers per response; several responses are checked against the fastkcv.max_gb budget (see kcv_engine()) left after the factorization, and the error message gives a batch size that fits.

Buffered leave-one-out

With buffer = r, observation \(i\) is held out together with every observation within Euclidean distance \(r\) of it (distance \(\le r\), computed on the coordinates as given, without any variogram anisotropy), and only \(i\) is predicted and reported. This removes the spatially correlated neighbors that make ordinary leave-one-out optimistic. buffer = 0 gives ordinary leave-one-out exactly.

Hold-out sets of neighboring points overlap, so each point is a separate kriging problem, solved from the same factorization with a hold-out set \(I\) of size \(m\), which needs the block \(Q_{II}\) of the matrix \(Q\) described in kcv_engine(). Two strategies are used, whichever needs fewer operations:

  • per point: form \(Q_{II}\) directly, about \(m^2 n\) operations per point and \(8 m n\) bytes of temporary memory (160 MB for \(m = 1000\), \(n = 20000\));

  • shared pairs: two points in a common hold-out set are at most \(2r\) apart, so the entries of \(Q\) for all pairs of points within \(2r\) are computed once (about \(n\) operations each, roughly \(2 \bar m n^2\) in total) and each \(Q_{II}\) is assembled from them. The cache takes 12 bytes per pair (about \(24 \bar m n\) bytes) and is used only if it fits, together with the factorization, in the fastkcv.max_gb budget (see kcv_engine()).

Each point also needs a Cholesky factorization of \(Q_{II}\) (\(m^3 / 3\) operations). Since \(m\) grows with the area of the buffer, large radii are expensive at large \(n\); targets restricts the predictions to a sample of points, at a proportional saving. These computations consist of many small matrix operations, which a multithreaded BLAS does not speed up and can slow down: with OpenBLAS, setting the environment variable OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 before starting R is usually as fast or faster. Use kcv_prepare() and kcv_run() to try several radii from one factorization.

An error names the first point that cannot be predicted: a buffer that holds out every observation, or (universal kriging) one that removes all observations that identify the trend, for example every observation of one level of a factor.

Performance

Almost all of the time goes into one dense Cholesky factorization and triangular inverse, which R delegates to its BLAS/LAPACK libraries. The reference BLAS shipped with many R builds is single-threaded and slow; an optimized BLAS is typically many times faster on these operations. Check which one R uses with extSoftVersion()["BLAS"] or sessionInfo().

  • Linux (Debian/Ubuntu): install an optimized BLAS such as OpenBLAS (sudo apt install libopenblas0-pthread); the system's alternatives mechanism switches R to it without reinstalling anything.

  • macOS: the CRAN build of R can use Apple's Accelerate framework; see the R for macOS FAQ for how to switch.

  • Windows: see "R Installation and Administration" for replacing R's BLAS.

Multithreaded BLAS libraries use all cores by default; when running several R processes in parallel, limit the threads (for OpenBLAS, the environment variable OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS). OpenBLAS starts one thread per logical CPU, and on CPUs with simultaneous multithreading (hyper-threading) one thread per physical core can be much faster: on a 4-core, 8-thread laptop, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=4 made 10-fold kcv() 1.6 to 2 times faster than the default at n = 1,500 to 5,000.

The factorization depends only on the locations, the model and the trend, not on the folds. To cross-validate several fold schemes for the same data, call kcv_prepare() once and kcv_run() for each scheme. Each fold of size \(m\) adds about \(m^2 n\) operations, so a few large folds cost the most: with 2 folds, the folds take about as long as the factorization.

See kcv_engine() for memory requirements.

Examples

library(sp)
data(meuse, package = "sp")
v <- gstat::vgm(0.59, "Sph", 897, 0.05)
cv <- kcv(log(zinc) ~ 1, ~ x + y, meuse, model = v)
head(cv)
#>   var1.pred  var1.var observed    residual      zscore fold      x      y
#> 1  6.769182 0.1800190 6.929517  0.16033461  0.37789233    1 181072 333611
#> 2  6.767296 0.1747339 7.039660  0.27236448  0.65157117    2 181025 333558
#> 3  6.296517 0.1818894 6.461468  0.16495146  0.38676967    3 181165 333537
#> 4  6.039217 0.2281430 5.549076 -0.49014098 -1.02616546    4 181298 333484
#> 5  5.581987 0.1743017 5.594711  0.01272471  0.03047874    5 181307 333330
#> 6  5.425952 0.2311933 5.638355  0.21240263  0.44174562    6 181390 333260
sqrt(mean(cv$residual^2))
#> [1] 0.3917495

# Buffered leave-one-out: neighbors within 300 m are held out too.
cv_buf <- kcv(log(zinc) ~ 1, ~ x + y, meuse, model = v, buffer = 300)
summary(cv_buf$n_heldout)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   1.000   7.000  10.000   9.981  13.000  19.000 
kcv_metrics(cv_buf)
#>     n      rmse       mae       bias     mean_z     var_z coverage_50
#> 1 155 0.5313131 0.4242791 0.04478428 0.06573575 0.7752399    0.516129
#>   coverage_80 coverage_90 coverage_95
#> 1   0.8903226   0.9290323   0.9612903

# The same statistics from a sample of 50 points.
set.seed(1)
kcv_metrics(kcv(log(zinc) ~ 1, ~ x + y, meuse, model = v, buffer = 300,
  targets = sample(nrow(meuse), 50)))
#>    n     rmse       mae         bias      mean_z     var_z coverage_50
#> 1 50 0.482048 0.3723308 -0.005066683 -0.01554473 0.6595127        0.58
#>   coverage_80 coverage_90 coverage_95
#> 1        0.92        0.96        0.98

# Several responses with the same model, trend and folds.
cv3 <- kcv(cbind(log(zinc), log(copper), log(lead)) ~ 1, ~ x + y, meuse,
  model = v, nfold = 5)
kcv_metrics(cv3)
#>      response   n      rmse       mae        bias      mean_z     var_z
#> 1   log(zinc) 155 0.4116874 0.3111180 0.004152948 0.008842182 0.8627269
#> 2 log(copper) 155 0.3143176 0.2505060 0.002310917 0.004644471 0.5196108
#> 3   log(lead) 155 0.4108739 0.3031579 0.005709850 0.011264441 0.8696293
#>   coverage_50 coverage_80 coverage_90 coverage_95
#> 1   0.5741935   0.8193548   0.9290323   0.9677419
#> 2   0.6258065   0.9354839   0.9677419   1.0000000
#> 3   0.6258065   0.8451613   0.9032258   0.9612903
